translations.a8c9929697315ae7a4256906: Replace the word “agent” with “new employee” and reread the 7 principles: nothing feels strange to someone who has already led others. Intention describes the role; context is onboarding; data is the official system; criteria are goals; autonomy is the scope of authority; observation is the report; supervision is the 1:1 meeting. The report on “the new era of AI” gave a new name to old practices.
translations.f8c1a946cdff9c6c1f477b21: People who think managing agents means learning everything from scratch get stuck before they even start. Realizing you already know a good part of the method removes fear and speeds up your first delegation. And it gives you a simple test: if you wouldn’t delegate like that to a person, don’t delegate like that to an AI.
translations.8589b5e7931d4d6bde56ed17: Onboarding: context—what you teach on day 1.
translations.265e5611a03e929fec5a8ff3: Scope of authority: autonomy—“up to R$ 500 you decide.”
translations.8201d80c70e81a11fa939c40: ⟪P0⟫2⟪P1⟫⟪P2⟫What the agent doesn’t “figure out on the fly”⟪P3⟫
translations.a83a3bdd579a737027f89ee0: A new employee infers a lot: they observe coworkers, notice the company tone, and ask in the hallway. The agent doesn’t do any of that; it works only with what’s written in the instructions and the data it has access to. Everything a person would infer has to become text: the tone, the source that counts, what to do when information is missing, and when to stop.
translations.0d26795b2ef0ac9d24a5ff2e: Most agent mistakes come from what “seemed obvious” to the person who delegated. With a person, lack of clarity costs a lot by going slowly; with an agent, it costs immediately and at scale. Listing the implicit is the cheapest way to avoid this mistake.
translations.1296c6940ec4b982ba4ee768: Tone: how you talk to a customer—formal or friendly.
translations.4c1232f9ea3d6a90ec963cf8: Source: which spreadsheet or system is the one that counts—and which one isn’t.
translations.b57bf9e49eadff8b0c393c17: If something is missing: what to do when the data doesn’t exist.
translations.8a9e642a76d873096698601d: Stop: what situation makes it call you.
translations.b8a1a7fe5d4b121d089ecc4b: ⟪P0⟫3⟪P1⟫⟪P2⟫People who program with agents already live this⟪P3⟫
translations.e480e06f1e9072c85ce5e65a: Code agents, like Claude Code and Codex, are AI programs that work inside a repository—the folder of a project with all its history. Anyone who uses these agents practices the 7 principles every day: the plan mode (the agent proposes before changing anything), the ⟪P0⟫ or ⟪P1⟫ (a file with the project rules), the repository as the source, tests (automated checks), permissions, failure log, and review.
translations.81d2ae96e84e026c3a18a8c8: This shows the method isn’t stage theory: it already works in production, in the hands of thousands of people. Even those who don’t program benefit by copying these practices into other areas. And programmers gain a vocabulary to explain their own routine to managers.
translations.6cf2651a50896fc621c4e5c3: ⟪P0⟫: context—the house rules in a file.
translations.14aa293efb11a57ec43db988: Tests: the readiness criterion—“done” is whatever passes the verification.
translations.054db246e882934898a6695a: ⟪P0⟫4⟪P1⟫⟪P2⟫Permission modes are the N0–N4 ladder with a button⟪P3⟫
translations.7c43c4ef50b96a6503f79fcc: In Claude Code, permission mode defines what the agent can do without asking. In plan, it only reads and proposes; in default, it asks for approval for every edit or command; in acceptEdits, it edits files on its own, but commands still ask; in bypassPermissions, it allows everything. It’s the same N0 to N4 autonomy ladder—just with a button instead of a conversation.
translations.f5a2cfe85d34af887bf4d4f7: Choosing the “on the fly” mode is the most common mistake people make when they start with code agents. With the ladder, the choice becomes rule-based: the level comes from the action and the risks, not from urgency. And it becomes clear what has to happen in order to move up a rung.
translations.28f6144c981cbc407e632494: N0 and N1: plan—only reads and proposes.
translations.d1a901c71a4f0366fe7457f9: N2: default—approves every edit and command.
translations.5d0c3137781ff62e4be47323: N3: acceptEdits—edits on its own; commands ask.
translations.527eef3fb4ffb05b86a89564: N4: only with hooks and isolated environment.
translations.96a37e0a143a7b9f0ab28d4a: ⟪P0⟫5⟪P1⟫⟪P2⟫Instructions, tests, and hooks: the method in production⟪P3⟫
translations.05ecff7c6545a7760e2b1965: Three pieces turn the principles into real configuration. The instruction file (⟪P0⟫ for the Claude Code, ⟪P1⟫ for Codex and others) sits at the root of the project and is read in every session. Tests are commands that automatically verify whether the work is correct. Hooks are triggers that run before an action and can block it; the allow and deny rules in the configuration grant or prohibit actions.
translations.1f50de6adbe158ce25599cb0: Writing “don’t deploy” in the conversation isn’t enough: the conversation ends and the rule disappears. In the instruction file, it applies every time; as a deny rule or hook, it applies even if the agent forgets. It’s the difference between asking and guaranteeing.
translations.aa27abdc5fc1e25916146d18: ⟪P0⟫: house rules read in every session.
translations.73b91555c6fb7849f976e3a6: Tests: a readiness criterion that doesn’t depend on opinion.
translations.427d9044daea7ac110ca6971: Deny: an action prohibited by permissions.
translations.e681a531982605ee635ec0d8: Hook: a lock that blocks the irreversible before it happens.
translations.12e7508c9c5822ab4a239c7c: The 7 questions are the same ones a good manager always asked. Without intention, the agent efficiently does the wrong task; without a source of truth, it picks the information on its own and picks badly; without criteria, it says “done” and you only find out later that it wasn’t. And the design of the principles is a circle: supervision feeds back into intention, each mistake becomes a rule, and each clean week becomes a rung of autonomy.
translations.e27068596a912b2acbaf92e4: Blaming “the AI” prevents you from fixing what’s within your reach: delegation. When you treat each error as a missing rule, the agent improves week after week without switching tools. The circle turns the Agent Sheet into a living process, not a form you fill out once.
translations.e7f32fb72b10809f86de7f6d: Without intention: it does the wrong task well.
translations.0e54dbc79d23086de58181b4: Without a source: it picks bad information.
translations.fbd26a635b49f7e2cc1212d3: Without criteria: a “done” that isn’t actually done.
translations.803e8d91b3dfd1c228a6a5ec: Circle: the observed error becomes a new rule.
translations.152c7ea6d4aa1b956d642e57: Take a real task from your choices through the first supervised week, and then through multiple agents.
translations.df6ac1e6631a78c7d8c3f111: The first agent in production should handle a frequent task, with visible output and cheap errors. Frequent, so you learn fast; visible, so you can check the result with your own eyes; cheap, so an error only costs a correction—not a customer. One task per sheet: if you came up with three, start with the one with the lowest risk.
translations.2e4d4223dc7733ff2664ed59: Starting with the most important process sounds ambitious, but it mixes risks and hides where the mistake was born. A small task gives, in a few days, real data to adjust the sheet. The confidence you earn from it is what unlocks the bigger tasks afterward.
translations.92babb6ca142d518f4ec476c: Frequent: it happens every week or every day.
translations.1c2d708af27bf0a23a6f7bf1: Visible: you check the result with your eyes.
translations.128e4dbd2d08835629c83a1d: Cheap error: a failure costs only a correction.
